Sons of Sceva
sunz uhv SEE-vuh
noun
From Greek huioi Skeua (G5207 + G4630); seven sons of one Sceva, a Jew and chief of the priests, who attempted to exorcise demons by the name of Jesus in Acts 19.

📖 Biblical Definition

The sons of Sceva were seven Jewish exorcists, sons of a man called a chief of the priests, who appear in Acts 19:13-16 during Paul's ministry at Ephesus. Marveling at the mighty works God wrought by the hands of Paul, these vagabond exorcists presumed to take the name of the Lord Jesus and use it as a magical formula, saying over those possessed with evil spirits, 'We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth.' But the evil spirit answered, 'Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye?' and the demoniac leaped upon them, overcame them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of the house naked and wounded. This terrifying scene teaches a doctrine the Reformed faith holds dear: the name of Jesus is not a charm to be wielded by the unbelieving, but a name that saves only those who truly trust in Him. The demons confess Christ's real authority and even know His true servant Paul, but they despise the pretender who has no living union with the Lord. Christ's power over the powers of darkness is real, but it is exercised through faith, not magic. The episode produced great fear, the magnifying of the name of the Lord Jesus, and the public burning of books of curious arts worth fifty thousand pieces of silver. It stands as a permanent rebuke to every superstitious abuse of holy things and to the presumption that the gospel can be borrowed without the new birth.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Seven Jewish would-be exorcists, sons of a chief priest, overpowered by a demon when they tried to use the name of Jesus as a magic charm.

SONS OF SCEVA, noun. From Greek huioi Skeua (G5207 + G4630); seven sons of Sceva, a Jew and chief of the priests at Ephesus.

Vagabond exorcists who attempted to cast out an evil spirit by adjuring it 'by Jesus whom Paul preacheth.'

The evil spirit answered, 'Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye?' and the man overcame them.

As it is written, 'And the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, and overcame them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded' (Acts 19:16).

A standing warning that the name of Jesus is no charm for the unbelieving but saves only the truly faithful.

📖 Key Scripture

Act 19:13 — "Then certain of the vagabond Jews, exorcists, took upon them to call over them which had evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth."

Act 19:14 — "And there were seven sons of one Sceva, a Jew, and chief of the priests, which did so."

Act 19:15 — "And the evil spirit answered and said, Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye?"

Act 19:16 — "And the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, and overcame them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The passage is misused by sensationalists who treat the name of Jesus as a power-formula, the very error the sons of Sceva committed and were judged for.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The abuse is older and more practical: deliverance ministries and superstitious practice that treat the name of Jesus as an incantation, repeating it as though syllables carried power apart from living faith. The sons of Sceva are the Bible's own refutation of such magic; the demon mocked them precisely because they had the formula without the faith.

The principle to recover is that Christ's authority over demons is genuine and that the unseen war is real, yet that authority is never transferable to the unconverted. Only those united to Christ by faith stand in His power. The name of Jesus saves the believer and terrifies the demon, but in the mouth of a stranger to grace it brings only shame, as Ephesus learned to its great fear and to the magnifying of the Lord.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek huioi Skeua (G5207 + G4630) names the seven sons of Sceva, Jewish exorcists rebuked at Ephesus.

expand to see more

Greek huios (G5207) — a son; here in the plural, the seven sons

Greek Skeuas (G4630) — Sceva, called a Jew and chief of the priests

Greek exorkistēs (G1845) — an exorcist, one who binds by an oath or adjuration

Greek horkizō (G3726) — to adjure, to charge by an oath, which they wrongly applied

The episode is set at Ephesus during Paul's mighty ministry recorded in Acts 19

Usage

"The sons of Sceva learned that the name of Jesus is no charm in the mouth of the unbelieving."

"Like those vagabond exorcists, every pretender who borrows the gospel without faith is exposed."

"The demon knew Paul but mocked the sons of Sceva, for Christ's power is wielded only through faith."
